--- title: "Working with real-world data" subtitle: "HWRS 564a · Week 12 · Tuesday, November 10" author: "Dr. Andrew Bennett" --- ## Today {.smaller} ::: {.kicker} Week 12, session 1 of 2 ::: 1. Quiz — five minutes 2. What an API is, and the `dataretrieval` package 3. Keeping a saved copy for when the API is down 4. Finding a site before you fetch its data 5. Streams: daily discharge at Sabino Creek 6. Wells: the same package, a different kind of record 7. A stream and a well on one time axis 8. Data sources beyond the USGS Most projects need several datasets, such as a stream gage, a few wells, and maybe a satellite product, and they rarely share the same time step or units. Today we pull a stream and a well from the USGS, put them on the same time axis, and look at where other kinds of data come from. # Getting data from an API {background-color="#AB0520"} ## A URL that returns data {.smaller} You can download a CSV from a website by clicking through it. An **API** (application programming interface) is a web address you build yourself that returns the data directly:
https://api.waterdata.usgs.gov/ogcapi/v0/collections/daily/items
?monitoring_location_id=USGS-09484000
&parameter_code=00060
&time=2024-10-01/2025-09-30
- underlined: the **endpoint**, which dataset you want (daily values) - blue: which **site** (Sabino Creek) · green: which **measurement** (discharge) · red: which **dates** - `?` starts the options and `&` separates them ::: {.fragment} Paste that into a browser and you get the data back as text. Because the request is written in your code, anyone can rerun it and get the same data, and changing the site or dates is a one-word edit. ::: ## `dataretrieval` builds the URL for you {.smaller} `dataretrieval` is the USGS's Python package for its water data. It builds the URL, sends the request, and turns the response into a pandas DataFrame. It is already installed in the course environment. ```python from dataretrieval import waterdata q, md = waterdata.get_daily( monitoring_location_id="USGS-09484000", parameter_code="00060", time="2024-10-01/2025-09-30", ) ``` Each call returns two things: the data (`q`, a DataFrame) and metadata (`md`). `md.url` is the exact URL that was sent. ::: {.fragment} **Use `waterdata`, not `nwis`.** Most tutorials online use `dataretrieval.nwis`. The USGS is retiring the services behind it: some `nwis` functions are deprecated and some, like `nwis.get_gwlevels`, no longer exist. If code from a tutorial fails because a function is missing, the tutorial is probably older than the package. ::: ## Reading a deprecation warning ``` DeprecationWarning: `nwis.get_record` is deprecated and will be removed from `dataretrieval` on or after 2027-05-06; use the appropriate `waterdata.get_*()` for the service you need instead. ``` ::: {.incremental} - It tells you **what** is going away - It tells you **when** - It tells you **what to use instead** ::: ::: {.fragment} A warning is not an error, and your code still runs. After the removal date, the same line raises an error, so it is worth switching when you first see the warning. ::: # When the API is down {background-color="#AB0520"} ## Why keep a saved copy A request can fail for reasons outside your code: - the USGS limits how many requests come from one IP address, and everyone on campus wifi shares one - large queries can time out even when the service is working - the network in the room may be slow or down Recent data is also **provisional** and can be revised after you download it. Every notebook in this course that calls an API also ships a saved copy of the data, so the lab works in class either way. ## The pattern {.smaller} ```python def load_sabino(): """Daily discharge at Sabino Creek. Live if possible, cached if not.""" try: q, md = waterdata.get_daily( monitoring_location_id="USGS-09484000", parameter_code="00060", statistic_id="00003", time="1990-10-01/2025-09-30") print(f"live from the USGS: {len(q):,} rows") return tidy(q) except Exception as exc: print(f"live fetch failed ({type(exc).__name__}); using the cached copy") return pd.read_csv(DATA / "cache" / "waterdata_09484000_daily.csv", parse_dates=["date"]) ``` ::: {.fragment} Both branches return **the same columns**, and the function prints which one ran, so a failed request is never silent. ::: ## Your turn: complete the fallback ```{pyodide} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_fallback def fetch_live(site): raise ConnectionError("the USGS is not answering") # pretend the API is down def read_cache(site): return f"cached data for {site}" ``` ```{pyodide} #| exercise: ex_fallback def load(site): try: return ______ except Exception as exc: print(f"live fetch failed ({type(exc).__name__}); using cache") return ______ load("USGS-09484000") ``` ::: {.hint exercise="ex_fallback"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint Try the live request first. If anything goes wrong, fall back to the cache. Both branches need a `return`. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_fallback"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```python try: return fetch_live(site) except Exception as exc: print(...) return read_cache(site) ``` Catching bare `Exception` usually hides bugs in your own code. Here it is reasonable: a network call can fail in many ways, and every one of them should end with the cached copy. ::: ::: ## Where the cache comes from A data file with no record of where it came from is hard to trust or update. The course cache is built by a script in the repository: ```bash python scripts/fetch_data.py --list # what gets built python scripts/fetch_data.py --week12 # rebuild today's files ``` ::: {.fragment} Every file in `data/cache/` was written by that script, so you can read exactly which request produced it. For your own projects, save the request alongside the data and note the date you pulled it. ::: # Finding the site {background-color="#0C234B"} ## Find sites first {.smaller} `dataretrieval.waterdata` mirrors how the USGS now organizes its data — by **collection**: | Function | Answers | |---|---| | `get_monitoring_locations` | what sites exist here? | | `get_time_series_metadata` | which of them measure what, and for how long? | | `get_daily` | daily summaries of a sensor record | | `get_continuous` | the raw sensor readings, every 15 minutes or so | | `get_field_measurements` | readings taken by hand, on a visit | ::: {.fragment} The first two are small and fast. Use them to pick a site before downloading a long record. ::: ## Your turn: which function? You need **groundwater levels** for a list of well IDs. `nwis.get_gwlevels` is gone. Pick the replacement. ```{pyodide} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_api descriptions = { "waterdata.get_daily": "daily summary values from a continuous sensor", "waterdata.get_continuous": "15-minute sensor readings", "waterdata.get_field_measurements": "discrete readings taken by hand in the field", "waterdata.get_samples": "laboratory water-quality analyses", } ``` ```{pyodide} #| exercise: ex_api choice = ______ print(f"{choice}: {descriptions[choice]}") ``` ::: {.hint exercise="ex_api"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint Most water levels in a basin monitoring network are measured by someone visiting the well with a tape a few times a year, not by a logger. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_api"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```python choice = "waterdata.get_field_measurements" ``` These are discrete, manual readings. `get_daily` and `get_continuous` return little or nothing for most wells, because few are instrumented. The wrong choice does not raise an error. It returns an empty DataFrame, so check `len(df)` after every request. ::: ::: ## Searching a box ```python from dataretrieval import waterdata series, md = waterdata.get_time_series_metadata( bbox=[-111.10, 32.15, -110.70, 32.40], # west, south, east, north parameter_code="72019", # depth to water below land surface ) ``` ::: {.fragment} | Well | Type | Depth (ft) | Daily record | |---|---|---|---| | `USGS-321208110525001` · C-045 | extensometer | 465 | 1979– | | `USGS-321517110571802` · WR-52 | extensometer | 808 | 1982– | | `USGS-321058110563301` · B-076 | extensometer | 885 | 1990– | | `USGS-321142110530301` · D-061 | extensometer | 1010 | 1990– | ::: ::: {.fragment} Many more wells in that box are measured by hand, but only **four** have a daily sensor record. All four are **extensometer wells**, which the USGS uses to monitor land subsidence. We'll come back to that at the end. ::: ## Your turn: IDs are strings {.smaller} The new API wants `"USGS-09484000"`: an **agency prefix**, and a **leading zero** that is part of the number — `int("09484000")` is a site that doesn't exist. Excel strips that zero when you open the file; so does `pd.read_csv` without `dtype={"site_no": str}`. Someone opened the site list in Excel. Turn it back into IDs the API accepts. ```{pyodide} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_ids raw = [9484000, 9485700, "321517110571802"] # two mangled gages, one well ``` ```{pyodide} #| exercise: ex_ids ids = [f"USGS-{str(s).zfill(______)}" for s in raw] print(ids) ``` ::: {.hint exercise="ex_ids"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint `"42".zfill(5)` is `"00042"` — it left-pads with zeros up to a width. Stream gage numbers are at least eight digits long. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_ids"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```python ids = [f"USGS-{str(s).zfill(8)}" for s in raw] # ['USGS-09484000', 'USGS-09485700', 'USGS-321517110571802'] ``` `zfill(8)` repairs the gages and leaves the 15-digit well number alone, because it is already longer than 8. The better fix is upstream: read the file with `dtype=str` so the zero is never lost. ::: ::: # Streams {background-color="#AB0520"} ## Daily discharge, the current way ```python q, md = waterdata.get_daily( monitoring_location_id="USGS-09484000", # Sabino Creek near Tucson parameter_code="00060", # discharge, ft³/s statistic_id="00003", # daily mean time="1990-10-01/2025-09-30", ) ``` ::: {.fragment} ``` ['time', 'value', 'unit_of_measure', 'approval_status', 'qualifier', 'parameter_code', 'statistic_id', 'monitoring_location_id', ...] ``` There is one `value` column, and **`parameter_code` and `unit_of_measure` tell you what it is**. All the `waterdata` functions return this same layout, so the same code works for streams and wells. (Older code using `nwis` gets a column called `00060_Mean` instead.) ::: ::: {.fragment} Once you have checked the parameter code and unit, rename the column when you load it, with the unit in the name: ```python q = q.rename(columns={"value": "discharge_cfs"}) ``` If the DataFrame looks wrong, paste `md.url` into a browser to see the raw response. ::: ## Sabino Creek, 35 water years ::: {#bd520228 .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week12_tue_real_world_data_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} If you only pull 2005–2024, the biggest day is a **monsoon** flood, 2,450 ft³/s on 31 July 2006. Over this longer range, the biggest day is in **January** 1993, during the winter storms. The date range you choose changes the answer, so always report it. ::: ## Your turn: water years Hydrologists total flow from **1 October to 30 September**, so winter storms and the spring runoff that follows are counted in the same year. Water year 2025 is October 2024 through September 2025. In pandas it is one line, because `True` counts as 1. ```{pyodide} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_wy import pandas as pd dates = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime( ["2024-09-30", "2024-10-01", "2025-01-08", "2025-09-30"])) ``` ```{pyodide} #| exercise: ex_wy wy = dates.dt.year + (dates.dt.month ______) pd.DataFrame({"date": dates.dt.date, "water_year": wy}) ``` ::: {.hint exercise="ex_wy"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint October, November, and December belong to the **next** calendar year's water year. Which months need the extra 1? ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_wy"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```python wy = dates.dt.year + (dates.dt.month >= 10) ``` 30 September 2024 is the last day of WY 2024; the next morning is WY 2025. `> 9` works too. `> 10` silently puts every October in the wrong year, and nothing errors. ::: ::: ## Annual runoff ::: {#995aea9c .cell fig-height='3.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week12_tue_real_world_data_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ft³/s × 0.0283 → m³/s, × 86,400 s → m³ per day, then sum by water year. ::: {.fragment} From **57.6** million m³ (1993) to **0.13** (2025): a 400-fold range. Water year 2025 was dry on 90% of days. The mean, 14.2, isn't close to most individual years. ::: # Wells {background-color="#0C234B"} ## Two ways a well gets measured {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **A sensor** - pressure transducer hung below the water surface - logs every 15–60 minutes, unattended - `get_daily`, `get_continuous` - can drift, so it's checked against hand measurements ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **A tape** - steel or electric tape, lowered by hand on a visit - a few readings a year, sometimes fewer - `get_field_measurements` - the reference the sensor is checked against ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Most wells only have the right-hand column. WR-52 has both, which lets us ask whether they agree. ::: ## One visit, five numbers {.smaller} ```python field, md = waterdata.get_field_measurements( monitoring_location_id="USGS-321517110571802") ``` | time | parameter_code | value | vertical_datum | |---|---|---|---| | 1983-11-04 22:00 | 62610 | 2211.69 | NGVD29 | | 1983-11-04 22:00 | 62611 | 2213.86 | NAVD88 | | 1983-11-04 22:00 | 72019 | 183.31 | Local Assumed Datum | ::: {.fragment} One water surface, three numbers: an elevation above two different datums, 2.2 ft apart, and a **depth below land surface**. Later visits add two more codes, `50012` and `70309` — extensometer compaction readings, not water at all. ::: ::: {.fragment .due-notice} `field["value"].mean()` runs fine and returns about 1,240 ft, an average of depths, elevations, and compaction readings that isn't meaningful. **Always filter on `parameter_code` first.** ::: ## Your turn: one parameter only ```{pyodide} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_param import pandas as pd field = pd.DataFrame({ "parameter_code": ["62610", "62611", "72019", "62610", "62611", "72019", "70309"], "value": [2211.69, 2213.86, 183.31, 2209.42, 2211.59, 185.58, 11.61], }) ``` ```{pyodide} #| exercise: ex_param depth = field[field["parameter_code"] == ______] print(f"{len(depth)} readings, mean depth {depth['value'].mean():.2f} ft") ``` ::: {.hint exercise="ex_param"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint Depth to water below land surface is `72019`. Look at the column's dtype — are the codes numbers or strings? ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_param"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```python depth = field[field["parameter_code"] == "72019"] ``` Two readings, mean 184.45 ft. Writing `72019` without quotes matches **nothing** — an integer never equals a string — and you get an empty frame and a `NaN` mean, not an error. Parameter codes are strings for the same reason site numbers are: `"00060"` as an integer is `60`. ::: ::: ## Depth is measured downward ::: {#f9295245 .cell fig-height='3.8' fig-width='11' execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week12_tue_real_world_data_files/figure-revealjs/cell-5-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} The water level dropped **35 ft** from 1991 to 2006, then rose **58 ft**. We flip the y-axis so that a rising water table goes up on the plot. ::: ## Do the sensor and the tape agree? On the 201 days that have both: ::: {.incremental} - median difference **0.06 ft** — under an inch - worst **4.2 ft**, on 17 January 2005 - the sensor record is corrected using these hand measurements, which is part of how it gets approved ::: ::: {.fragment} Gaps matter too. The sensor ran all 365 days of WY 2017, but only **103** days of WY 2014. An average from 103 days isn't comparable to one from a full year, so check how many days each year has before averaging. ::: # Two records, one axis {background-color="#AB0520"} ## Annual runoff and annual depth ::: {#246278a0 .cell fig-height='4.6' fig-width='11' execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](week12_tue_real_world_data_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Wet years like 1993 and 1995 don't show up in the well. The correlation between annual runoff and the change in depth is only **r ≈ 0.2**. The rise after 2006 matches when Tucson Water cut pumping from its central wellfield and switched to recharged Colorado River water, starting in 2001. WR-52 is 808 ft deep and about 15 km from Sabino Creek, so it mostly reflects **pumping**, not this stream. ::: ## Lining up two records ::: {.due-notice} Two records that look related on a plot aren't necessarily connected. The data can show whether they change together; explaining why takes physical reasoning. ::: # Beyond the USGS {background-color="#0C234B"} ## Points and grids {.smaller} | | In situ | Remote sensing / gridded | |---|---|---| | What it is | a sensor at a place | a pixel over an area | | Shape | table: time × site | array: time × y × x | | Python | `pandas` | `xarray` (+ `rioxarray` for GeoTIFFs) | | Strength | direct, long records | covers areas with no wells or gages | | Catch | only where someone chose to measure | footprint, revisit time, and it is a *retrieval* — a model's estimate, not a reading | ::: {.fragment} You usually need both. A satellite can show that a region is losing water; a well shows what is happening at one location. ::: ## In situ sources worth knowing {.smaller} | Source | What | Access | |---|---|---| | [ADWR GWSI](https://azwatermaps.azwater.gov/gwsiweb/) | Arizona's well inventory and water levels — far more wells than the USGS holds here | web map + bulk download | | [Water Quality Portal](https://www.waterqualitydata.us/) | chemistry from USGS, EPA, and states | `dataretrieval.wqp`, `waterdata.get_samples` | | [NRCS SNOTEL](https://wcc.sc.egov.usda.gov/awdbRestApi/swagger-ui/index.html) | snow water equivalent, soil moisture | REST API | | [ACIS](https://www.rcc-acis.org/docs_webservices.html) / [GHCN-Daily](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/global-historical-climatology-network-daily) | station precipitation and temperature | web services | | [AZMET](https://azmet.arizona.edu/) | UA's agricultural weather network, reference ET | web + API | | [AmeriFlux](https://ameriflux.lbl.gov/) | eddy-covariance ET and carbon flux towers | download, free account | | [HydroShare](https://www.hydroshare.org/) | datasets other researchers published | web + Python client | ## Remote sensing and gridded sources {.smaller} | Source | Measures | Scale | |---|---|---| | [GRACE / GRACE-FO](https://grace.jpl.nasa.gov/) | change in total water storage, groundwater included | a few hundred km, monthly, 2002– | | [InSAR — NASA OPERA](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/data/projects/opera), [ADWR subsidence](https://www.azwater.gov/hydrology/field-services/land-subsidence-arizona) | ground motion: subsidence from pumping | tens of metres, every few weeks | | [OpenET](https://openetdata.org/) | evapotranspiration from Landsat | 30 m, monthly, western US | | [SMAP](https://nsidc.org/data/smap) | surface soil moisture, top ~5 cm | 9–36 km, every 2–3 days | | [AppEEARS](https://appeears.earthdatacloud.nasa.gov/) | MODIS, Landsat, and more, clipped to your points or polygon | whatever the product is | | [Planetary Computer](https://planetarycomputer.microsoft.com/catalog) | Landsat, Sentinel, DEMs, climate, as a searchable catalog | per product | | [PRISM](https://prism.oregonstate.edu/), [Daymet](https://daymet.ornl.gov/), [gridMET](https://www.climatologylab.org/gridmet.html) | gridded precipitation, temperature, reference ET | 0.8–4 km, daily | ::: {.fragment} The four extensometer wells from earlier are used to check InSAR subsidence maps. Ground and satellite data are most useful together. ::: ## Python tools for the rest {.smaller} | Tool | Use it for | |---|---| | [`dataretrieval`](https://doi-usgs.github.io/dataretrieval-python/) | USGS water data and the Water Quality Portal — today | | [`earthaccess`](https://earthaccess.readthedocs.io/) | searching and downloading NASA Earthdata: GRACE, SMAP, MODIS, OPERA (free login) | | [`pystac-client`](https://pystac-client.readthedocs.io/) | searching STAC imagery catalogs such as Planetary Computer | | [HyRiver](https://docs.hyriver.io/) | `py3dep` elevation, `pydaymet` / `pygridmet` climate, `pynhd` flowlines | | [`xarray`](https://docs.xarray.dev/) / [`rioxarray`](https://pypi.org/project/rioxarray/) | gridded arrays with labelled dimensions; GeoTIFFs | | [Earth Engine](https://earthengine.google.com/) | analysis on Google's servers over the whole archive (account required) | ::: {.fragment} `xarray` is already in the course environment. The others are not — add them with `uv add` in your own project, not in this repo. ::: ## Your turn: what does one pixel see? A GRACE grid cell is roughly 300 km on a side. Arizona is 295,000 km². ```{pyodide} #| setup: true #| exercise: ex_footprint arizona_km2 = 295_000 grace_side_km = 300 ``` ```{pyodide} #| exercise: ex_footprint grace_cell_km2 = ______ n_cells = arizona_km2 / grace_cell_km2 print(f"one GRACE cell ≈ {grace_cell_km2:,} km²") print(f"Arizona ≈ {n_cells:.1f} GRACE cells") ``` ::: {.hint exercise="ex_footprint"} ::: {.callout-note collapse="false"} ## Hint A square's area is its side squared. ::: ::: ::: {.solution exercise="ex_footprint"} ::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"} ## Solution ```python grace_cell_km2 = grace_side_km ** 2 # 90,000 km² ``` Arizona is only about **three GRACE cells**. GRACE can show regional groundwater loss, but it can't resolve the Tucson basin or a single well. Choose data whose resolution matches your question. ::: ::: ## Five questions for any new dataset ::: {.incremental} 1. **What** exactly was measured — parameter, unit, datum, sign convention? 2. **Where**, and over what footprint — a point, a pixel, a basin? 3. **When**, how often, and what's missing? 4. **Measured or modelled?** A retrieval is an estimate with its own error. 5. **Provisional or final** — and on what date did you pull it? ::: ::: {.fragment} Each of these came up today: vertical datums, pixel size, the 103-day year, and approval status. ::: ## Wrap up {.smaller} ::: {.kicker} What you did today ::: - Read a deprecation warning and switched from `nwis` to `waterdata` - Wrote a fallback that loads a saved copy when the API request fails - Discovered sites with metadata before fetching data - Pulled a stream (`get_daily`) and a well (`get_daily`, `get_field_measurements`) from one API, with IDs and parameter codes kept as strings - Totalled flow by water year and plotted depth the right way up - Lined up two records and discussed what they do and don't show - Mapped where in situ and remote-sensing data live, and the tools to reach them ::: {.kicker} Lab ::: - `labs/week12/week12_lab_pinal_water_levels.ipynb`: download every USGS water level in the Pinal AMA, clean it, and compare the trends with the Pinal model
